To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the carboxy-terminal tail of the Sindbis virus E2 membrane protein is initially translocated to the cytoplamsic face of the endoplamic reticulum and subsequently returned to the cytoplasmic face after the E2 protein has been incorporated into the virion membrane.
the cytoplasmically oriented carboxyl terminal tail of a type I viral membrane protein is translocated into cellular membranes and then returned to the cytosol.

the carboxy terminal domain of the alphavirus E2 glycoproteins is initially exposed on the cytoplasmatic side of the membrane, but is translocated to the lumen of endoplasmic and Golgi membranes, and that the translocation of this domain is required for the assembly of alphavirus virions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular biology of the alphavirus group of viruses, and in particular with the Sindbis virus.
the molecular biology of viruses that cause human diseases such as polio, measles, rabies and AIDS, and with their interaction with the human immune system.
understanding the molecular mechanisms of virus assembly, which is an important step in the life-cycle of all viruses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the E2 glycoproteins of Sindbis virus are translocated from the cytoplasm into the ER membrane and are returned to the cytosol after export of the glycoproteins from the ER.

the cytoplasmically located carboxyl termini of E2 are transiently translocated to the ER lumen, and are returned to the cytosol, after which they are translocated to the plasma membrane, where they remain.

the E2 glycoproteins of Sindbis virus are initially inserted into the endoplasmatic reticulum membrane with the carboxyl terminal cytoplasmic domain oriented to the cytosolic side of the membrane and then the cytoplasmically oriented carboxyl terminal domains are translocated to the lumenal side of the endoplamic reticulum membrane.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cytoplasm is a dynamic environment for the assembly of viral membranes.
we have demonstrated that a cytoplasmically oriented tail is translocated into the membrane and then returned to the cytosol, and this translocation is required for the assembly of the virus.
the E2 glycoproteins are initially translocated in a manner similar to other secreted proteins and that they are then returned to the cytosolic face of the membrane.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the E2 tail can act as a signal sequence for the export of other viral proteins, but it is not a signal sequence for its own integration into the ER membrane.

the cytoplasmically oriented carboxyl termini of type I membrane proteins are translocated into membranes during synthesis, and that the orientation of the cytoplamic tail is not a fixed feature of the protein.
the E2 cytoplasmic domain is translocated into cellular membranes during the synthesis and assembly of Sindbis virus.
